country.comment: Study examines national sanitation policy (1994–2014) and municipal implementation in the City of Cape Town (CoCT), South Africa.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, and Introduction; PDF p. 2, Methods

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative policy implementation case study; no quantitative point estimates, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Assessing 14 years (2001–2014) of Free Basic Sanitation (FBSan) implementation in Cape Town's informal settlements, the study finds that failure to achieve universal household sanitation access resulted not solely from municipal maladministration, but from ambiguous national policy definitions, a policy and regulatory vacuum regarding informal settlements and shared/communal sanitation, legal and physical constraints preventing waterborne sewerage or VIP latrines on occupied high-density land, funding gaps (inability to use housing grants in informal areas and unbudgeted O&M/security expenses), inter-departmental silos and restructuring fatigue, officials deferring project-level discretion to avoid personal financial liability under the 1999 Public Finance Management Act, and breakdown of assumed community self-help management. Difficulty establishing indigent eligibility criteria led the City of Cape Town (CoCT) to extend free basic water and sanitation broadly, and shared-toilet disrepair alongside resident protests and civil society advocacy prompted CoCT in 2013 to reformulate local policy by introducing a municipal janitorial service (contracting residents for on-site O&M), shifting shared-facility responsibility from households to the municipality while South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) recommendations lacked legislative or regulatory enforcement power.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 5–8, Results and Discussion; PDF p. 9, Conclusions

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed) and capped at 2 by the qualitative study design ceiling (CASP). Through 9 months of embedded participant observation inside 3 municipal offices, 10 months of observation at an informal settlement ablution block, semi-structured interviews, and municipal file review, the author directly observed administrative mechanisms (indigent eligibility difficulties, land occupation/legal barriers to sewerage, departmental silos/veto points, PFMA personal liability risk deterring street-level discretion, and lack of SAHRC regulatory enforcement authority) shaping sanitation delivery.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 1–2, Methods; PDF pp. 5–8, Results and Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines occupied-land/informal-settlement tenancy and legal constraints on installing waterborne sewerage vs constitutional obligation to serve regardless of tenancy (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, property, planning); lifeline tariffs, cross-subsidies, free O&M disputes, multi-departmental veto/clearance points, and consensus/approval delays (BURDEN: fees, procedural_steps, delay); street-level vs senior-management discretion, indigent targeting challenges, local policy accommodations including universal free provision and municipal janitorial services, and community consultation/self-help participation (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion, hardship_exception, accommodation, participation); and SAHRC human-rights complaints, PFMA personal financial liability vs weak national/SAHRC regulatory sanctions, municipal departmental silos/restructuring and national institutional shuffling, and DA-ANC partisan dynamics (ENFORCEMENT: complaint, sanction, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).

outcome_flags.comment: Primary empirical outcomes examined are informal-settlement basic and shared sanitation access (sanitation_access), installation of conventional/alternative waterborne sewerage connections (formal_connection), settlement servicing ratios and coverage expansion (service_coverage), toilet functionality/disrepair and janitorial improvements in reliability (service_reliability), cleanliness, privacy/dignity of unenclosed or bucket toilets, and safety (service_quality), Free Basic Sanitation lifeline subsidies and free O&M affordability for the poor (affordability), and rollout/decision delays from intra-community tensions, partisan politics, and multi-departmental clearance points (delay). Free Basic Water access is also briefly discussed as policy background and in relation to Cape Town's indigent eligibility policy (PDF pp. 3, 5, 9).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative longitudinal case study. Although the author uses the phrase 'mixed method for multiphase longitudinal studies' (PDF p. 1), this refers to triangulating three qualitative data sources (desktop document review, semi-structured interviews, and participant observation); there is no quantitative primary empirical component, so CASP Qualitative Checklist applies rather than MMAT.

sample_size.value: 1 municipality case study (City of Cape Town); 4 interviews with national policymakers (April 2015); unspecified number of semi-structured interviews with residents, municipal officials, activists and academics (March 2010–August 2013); participant observation in 3 City of Cape Town offices (9 months, March 2010–September 2012) and 1 ablution block in BM Section informal settlement (November 2012–August 2013); plus secondary desktop document review (1994–2014)

study_design.comment: Qualitative case study applying an adapted Mazmanian and Sabatier (1989) policy implementation framework to 14 years (2001–2014) of Cape Town informal-settlement sanitation programming using qualitative document review, semi-structured interviews, and participant observation.
study_design.value: Qualitative longitudinal policy implementation case study combining secondary desktop document review, semi-structured interviews, and participant observation (described by the author as a mixed method for multiphase longitudinal studies)

evidence_quotes.quote: Received 2 January 2018; accepted in revised form 20 September 2019

An assessment of national policy and implementation in South Africa’s second largest city (Cape Town) indicated that irreconcilable differences between municipal officials, residents and advocates’ interpretations of broadly-framed national policy, as well as policy gaps specific to servicing informal settlements and providing shared sanitation, contributed to the municipality’s failure to achieve policy objectives.

The author interviewed 4 national policymakers in April 2015, and conducted semi-structured interviews with residents, municipal officials, activists and academics involved in policy design, implementation and advocacy from March 2010 to August 2013.

The author also collected data as a participant observer in three CoCT offices for 9 months from March 2010 to September 2012, and at an ablution block in BM Section informal settlement from November 2012 to August 2013.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 5, Results and Discussion (Financial allotment)
evidence_quotes.quote: CoCT (2001 p. 11) additionally provided free water and sanitation to all residents due to the challenge of establishing eligibility criteria for indigent households.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 6, Results and Discussion (Implementation capability)
evidence_quotes.quote: Municipalities are constitutionally compelled to provide all South Africans with access to services, irrespective of land tenancy. CoCT officials hence were obliged to provide sanitation access despite the national government’s intention of eradicating all informal settlements by 2014.
